analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 39 senators including the Senate majority leader, was referred to the Senate labor committee in April 2021 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (seven days) a year. The leave could be used for a worker's own illness, doctor visits, caring for a sick child or family member, or handling domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Very small employers could opt out of paying for it, but would have to offer the same 56 hours as unpaid leave. The bill also makes it illegal for an employer to fire or punish someone for using the leave, and gives the Labor Department and workers the power to enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 29 percent of private-sector workers who lack any paid sick time, especially low-wage workers — 55 percent of the lowest-paid quarter of private workers have none — and workers in food service, more than 80 percent of whom lack access. It also helps parents who must send sick children to school or daycare, workers who need preventive medical care, and survivors of domestic violence who need time to see a doctor, relocate, or go to court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers with no paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least one hour of earned paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for a worker's own illness, medical care, care for family members, or needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Employers with fewer than 15 employees may opt out of the paid requirement but must still provide at least 56 hours of unpaid sick leave a year.

The bill makes it unlawful for employers to interfere with, restrain, or deny these rights, including retaliating against workers who use the leave, and gives employees a right to sue and directs the Department of Labor to investigate complaints.

The bill's findings note that workers without paid sick days are more likely to work while sick, forgo medical care, send sick children to school, and suffer workplace injuries, and that city paid-sick-time laws were associated with modest drops in influenza rates.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who bear the cost of paid leave not worked — the expense falls hardest on industries that employ many low-wage workers without current sick leave, such as restaurants, retail, and hospitality. Businesses with existing leave policies that already meet the standard owe nothing new.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a new labor cost for employers, and it falls most heavily on restaurants, retail, and other businesses with thin margins and many hourly workers who currently get no sick leave.

Workers at the smallest employers would get only unpaid leave, since firms with fewer than 15 employees can opt out of paying for it — so the lowest-wage workers at tiny businesses would have the right to stay home but no pay while doing so.

The benefit is capped at 56 hours a year and no cash payout is required when a worker leaves a job, so it is a floor rather than comprehensive leave; employers with existing adequate policies owe nothing beyond what they already provide.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers with no paid sick time, the gain is direct and immediate: seven paid days a year to see a doctor or care for a sick child without losing pay or a job. The main cost is a real one — paid leave is a genuine expense for labor-intensive employers — and the bill's carve-out letting the smallest firms off with unpaid leave means the protection is thinnest where pay is lowest. On balance the bill's design is modest and careful: it sets a low cap, exempts no-cost existing policies, defers to more generous state laws, and includes anti-retaliation enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2021 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the Healthy Families Act on April 15, 2021, joined by 37 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer.
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That was the bill's last action of any kind. Over the remaining 21 months of the 117th Congress, the committee held no hearing or markup and the full Senate never voted on it.

No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, so its support was entirely within the Democratic caucus at a time when the Senate was split 50-50 and most legislation required at least some Republican votes to advance.

The bill would have required employers with 15 or more employees to provide up to 56 hours of earned paid sick leave a year, with an unpaid-leave option for smaller employers and anti-retaliation and Labor Department enforcement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly those in retail, food service, and hospitality with many hourly workers, are better off because no federal paid-sick-leave mandate was ever enacted, and workers without paid sick days remain where they started.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act in the Senate in April 2021.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and it was never brought to the floor while Republicans could have offered support.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents — 35 of 48 Senate Democrats and both independents — and not a single one of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on; the bill then died in committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: These industries employ the largest share of workers without paid sick time — more than 80 percent of food-preparation and serving workers lack access — so the bill would have added a direct paid-leave cost for them. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the workers whose leave it would have guaranteed.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees generally
industries.note: Any covered employer would owe paid sick leave up to 56 hours a year, though firms with existing adequate policies owe nothing new. Businesses that already provide such leave would face little or no added cost.
Small employers could opt out of the paid requirement but must still offer 56 hours of unpaid leave, giving them flexibility while leaving their workers with a right to time off but no pay for it.
